summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory and stands under the United States federal framework, which applies on the island in full. The territory's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

Law 63 of 2025, the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors in Puerto Rico, was signed in July 2025. Its Article 4 prohibition is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: neither may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor under the pretext of a gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

The Article 3 definition of banned chemical and surgical mutilation is drafted more broadly than the prohibition it supports. It expressly covers the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used for the purpose of treating gender dysphoria, and it defines a child or minor as any person under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law with a fixed 15-year term, permanent licence loss for professionals, and a $50,000 fine per violation for legal entities.

Legal analysis of that drafting identifies a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient use, the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty clause says any person. Under standard criminal doctrines, a definition creates no offence by itself, the principle of legality bars analogy, and a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation, so a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of their parents for enabling it, would almost certainly fail. The textual ambiguity is nonetheless what legal advocates flag as the statute's chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer arriving only after the fact.

For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is that carrying and prescribed hormones sit inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and that no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ban closes off gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto the bill, stating that it criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez noted that the bill disregards the specialist consultation process preceding parental authorisation of puberty blockers or hormonal treatments and criminalizes it instead; Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona stated that the measure directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April 2025, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés, and was re-approved on 28 June. The Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico all registered opposition, and the Federation announced plans to challenge the law in court.

Reporting on the enactment adds that the law was pushed through non-public hearings, that it mandates Education and Health department campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care, and that the amendments proposed by Health Secretary Ramos Otero to allow puberty blockers and continuation of existing treatment were not adopted. The report characterises the enacted text as the most extreme care restriction in United States jurisdictions. Amnesty International, JURIST and the Associated Press independently record the July 2025 signing, the under-21 scope, and the 15-year sentence and $50,000 penalty.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminal. Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002; after the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

Discrimination protection is partial. An anti-discrimination bill covering sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing passed the House 43-6 in November 2009, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass, Senate Bill 238 signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 pairing of a religious freedom bill with a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval and sustained protests. A separate 2019 bill banning conversion therapy for minors, SB1000, passed the Senate and had governor support but died when the pro-statehood NPP caucus blocked a floor vote in the House.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a United States territory, and no separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or ruling was located. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, directs federal agencies including the Bureau of Prisons to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth. The ACLU reported that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds; advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was secured through federal court: four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit filed in Puerto Rico in March 2014, with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening, one couple having married in Canada in 2007 and another in New York in 2012, and a former National Guard member among the plaintiffs.
tangentialFactors:
The care ban is described in reporting as the most extreme such restriction in United States jurisdictions, a comparison drawn from the statute's under-21 scope, its fixed 15-year penalty and its facilitation language rather than from any ranking of enforcement outcomes.

Puerto Rico's legislative record on adjacent questions is contested rather than settled. The 2019 conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support, the religious freedom pairing was withdrawn amid protests, and a 2017 religious freedom bill was vetoed, while the 2025 care ban passed both chambers with only the amendments proposed by the Health Secretary as a point of friction.

The 2020 hate-crime prosecutions and the January 2021 state of emergency concern violence against transgender people on the island and are recorded here as evidence of the enforcement environment, not as a measure of current risk magnitude; no per-capita or population-adjusted figure is available in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents under 21 are barred from gender-affirming medical treatment, and medical institutions, health professionals and legal entities face a fixed 15-year term, permanent licence loss and a $50,000 fine per violation. The professional bodies that opposed the bill, including the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling and the Bar Association, are the licensing and standards bodies their members answer to.

Resident families face the facilitation language directly: the ACLU of Puerto Rico's position is that the bill criminalizes parents who authorise treatment, and the statute's penalty clause reads as any person who violates the law. The law also mandates Education and Health department campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care, which shapes what resident students and patients will be told by public institutions.

Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is covered by the 2013 law, but public facilities, transportation, business transactions and housing were stripped from the bill before passage and remain uncovered by territorial statute. Hate crime charges became available in 2020, when the first charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought over the April 2020 murders of two transgender women, and the territory is covered by the federal hate-crime statute as well.

In federal custody, transgender inmates are housed by sex assigned at birth under the January 2025 executive order, and the Bureau of Prisons no longer reports how many transgender people it holds. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or ruling was located, so residents held territorially rather than federally are governed by an unsourced gap.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Article 6 of Law 63 of 2025 can reach a patient using prescribed hormones, or a parent enabling that use, is unresolved: no test case had been located at the time of writing, and the sources present the drafting tension as an open question rather than a settled construction.

The outcome of the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico's announced court challenge to the ban is not sourced here, nor is any territorial or federal ruling on the law's constitutionality.

No Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy, special unit or judicial ruling on trans-inmate housing was located, so territorial custody practice apart from the federal framework is not sourced.

The sources give no per-capita or population-adjusted figure for violence against transgender people in Puerto Rico, and no denominator against which the 2020 killings and the January 2021 state of emergency could be ranked against other jurisdictions.

Whether the 2025 law's mandated departmental campaigns have been issued, and in what form, is not sourced.
